risks: Q1 (blocking) has no recorded human answer, and the clarification's proposed answer — the Referer reduced to a registrable domain — is not buildable: feasibility evidence shows no public-suffix list on the classpath and A1 forbids adding one. T7 therefore stores the canonicalised full host per feasibility's recommended option (U1). Because A3 rules out backfill, this choice is permanent for every row written before it is revisited. A reviewer must confirm 'full host is fine' or approve a PSL dependency at the design gate.

Q2 (blocking) has no recorded human answer. The plan takes only phase 1 of the impact analysis's mitigation: the aggregate /actuator/health keeps its current membership and Redis stays gating on it. If some platform outside this repository is routing on that aggregate, the service continues to amplify a Redis blip into a fleet-wide outage — i.e. AC3 remains partially unmet by design until whoever owns the deployment manifests confirms the probe is repointed at /actuator/health/readiness. U6 (whether readiness should include PostgreSQL) is unresolved for the same reason and is deliberately not acted on.

T3 depends on U3: with no Spring Security filter chain, a health group inherits show-details: when-authorized and 'authorized' is never satisfied, so the dependencies group must be set to show-details: always to satisfy AC2. Actuator shares the public port 8080 and no ingress rule exists in this repository, so as planned this publishes 'redis is DOWN' to any caller. A8's internal-only assumption is unverified and is the load-bearing part of AC2's design.

T7/T8 sit inside RedirectController's catch(RuntimeException) -> notFound() block: a derivation or counter defect converts live 302s into 404s with no 5xx on any dashboard and no counted click. This failure is invisible to error-rate monitoring and would first surface as a customer reporting vanished campaign traffic.

T8's origin keyspace must stay disjoint from clicks:pending. If origin fields land in that hash, old pods running read_click_deltas.lua during a rolling deploy HDEL zero-valued fields and discard non-UUID fields with a WARN, corrupting the durable+pending invariant that AC7's clickCount rests on — and single-instance tests would all pass.

T4's breaker must not cover ResolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing, the service's only deliberate 503. A breaker there keeps refusing creates for the whole open window after Redis recovers, lengthening an outage the change exists to shorten, and suppresses the eviction that makes issuing a code safe.

T9 puts a second writer in the flush transaction. A rollup row that fails permanently rolls back links.addClicks for that link, so its delta stays pending forever and its clickCount silently stops advancing; conversely a rollup failure that skips counter.settle() double-counts clicks. Both are AC7 regressions with no external error signal.
T6's V5 migration must be applied before any pod maps the new entity: ddl-auto is validate, so an image deployed ahead of the migration fails to start outright rather than degrading.

T8's distinct-origin cap is the only defence against attacker-controlled cardinality: Referer is unvalidated on an unauthenticated route with a 3000/min/IP bucket, so without the cap one sweep mints unbounded Redis fields and rollup rows, starving the 500-entry flush batch. U2 fixes no number; the plan assumes the storage cap equals the response top-N.

T11 mounts the customer-wide aggregate at /api/v1/analytics rather than /api/v1/links/analytics because a literal path under /api/v1/links/ would shadow GET /api/v1/links/{code} for any existing link whose code is 'analytics' — permitted by the alias charset and absent from RESERVED_CODES. If design moves it back under /api/v1/links, that collision returns silently.

The two increments are planned as independently deployable (A13), but T2 and T4 both edit RedisClickCounter and ResolutionCache while T8 and T9 edit the same click and flush classes. Landing them out of order, or in one release, concentrates unrelated risk on the highest-volume path.
